title: Which Popular Customer Experience Statistics Have No Real Source?
summary: Which popular CX statistics have no real source? "96% never complain" has none, "5x cheaper to retain" is a 1980s estimate. What to cite instead.
body_markdown:
Open almost any customer experience (CX) business case and you'll find the same four numbers. Ninety-six percent of unhappy customers never complain. A 5% lift in retention raises profits by 25% to 95%. Acquiring a customer costs five times more than keeping one. And lately, 95% of AI pilots fail. They show up in board decks, vendor pitches and analyst summaries, usually with a one-word citation.


Here's the short answer. The "96% never complain" and "1 in 26 complain" figures have no traceable primary source at all. The "5x cheaper to retain" ratio traces back to a late-1980s estimate, not a published measurement. The "25% to 95%" profit range is Frederick Reichheld's own, but it is repeated without the scope behind it. The AI failure rates are real reports with weak derivations, or forecasts quoted as outcomes. Thematic traced each one to its origin for this piece. For every one, there's a peer-reviewed or primary source you can cite instead.


This matters because a CFO who checks one number will stop trusting the rest. Below: how these statistics spread, what each one actually traces to, and what to put in your deck instead.


## How do CX statistics lose their source?


A number starts life with a scope: an industry, a decade, a sample, a definition. A secondary source quotes it without the scope. A third source quotes the second and cites the original, which it hasn't read. A few rounds later, the number is "from Bain" or "from Harvard," and nobody in the chain has opened the source.


Statistics listicles speed this up. Customer Service Manager Magazine's facts page, for example, attributes the "26 remain silent" line to "Lee Resource Inc" and the 96% line to "Understanding Customers" by Ruby Newell-Legner. Neither citation includes a method, a sample size or a date. Other pages credit the 96% figure to 1st Financial Training Services. Three origins for one family of numbers usually means none.


Numbers also migrate.[Shep Hyken's 2020 Achieving Customer Amazement Study](https://www.forbes.com/sites/shephyken/2020/07/12/ninety-six-percent-of-customers-will-leave-you-for-bad-customer-service/) found that 96% of more than 1,000 consumers were at least somewhat willing to switch brands for better service. That's a real survey. It says nothing about complaining. But a 96% figure about switching and a 96% figure about silence are easy to merge, and they have been.


## Which CX statistics fail a source check?


**Statistic as usually quoted** **What it actually traces to** **Verdict** **Cite instead**


96% of unhappy customers never complain / 1 in 26 complain Facts pages and listicles; no study, method or sample No real source 2025 National Customer Rage Survey; Stephens and Gwinner (1998)


5% more retention = 25% to 95% more profit Reichheld's Bain research: *Harvard Business Review* , 1990, on service businesses; the exact range in his 2001 book *Loyalty Rules!* Real origin, scope dropped Gupta, Lehmann and Stuart, *Journal of Marketing Research* , 2004


Acquisition costs 5x retention A late-1980s TARP estimate, popularized in 1990 Rule of thumb, not a measurement Your own acquisition and retention costs


95% of AI pilots fail / 80% of AI projects fail MIT NANDA 2025 report; RAND quoting a 2022 press estimate Weak derivation or second-hand Gartner's dated forecasts, labeled as forecasts


**"96% of unhappy customers never complain."** This is the weakest of the four. The citation chain runs through blog posts and a 2015 listicle to an analyst attribution with nothing underneath it. No research report containing the figure appears to exist.


The sourced alternative makes the same point with less exposure. The[2025 National Customer Rage Survey](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/new-national-customer-rage-survey-reveals-civility-in-freefall-across-americas-marketplace-302629849.html) comes from Customer Care Measurement and Consulting (CCMC) with Arizona State University's (ASU) W. P. Carey School of Business. It found that 77% of U.S. consumers had a product or service problem in the past 12 months. That rate has more than doubled since 1976. The survey estimates more than $596 billion in future revenue losses from ineffective complaint handling. One in four complainants posted about their most serious problem on social media. Of those, 43% said the company never responded.


For the silence itself, cite Nancy Stephens and Kevin Gwinner's work on noncomplaining in the *Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science* (1998). ASU's write-up of their research states that[up to two-thirds of customers](https://news.wpcarey.asu.edu/20060927-penny-your-thoughts-when-customers-dont-complain) do not report their dissatisfaction. Quote it as "up to," because the paper is a model of complaint behavior built on interviews, not a prevalence survey.


**"A 5% increase in retention raises profits 25% to 95%."** This one has a real origin, which is why it survives. Frederick Reichheld and W. Earl Sasser published "[Zero Defections: Quality Comes to Services](https://hbr.org/1990/09/zero-defections-quality-comes-to-services) " in *Harvard Business Review* in 1990. The article made its case from service businesses.[Bain's summary of it](https://www.bain.com/insights/zero-defections-quality-comes-to-services-harvard-business-review-hbr/) says companies can boost profits by "almost 100%" by retaining just 5% more of their customers.


The exact range comes from Reichheld himself.[His 2001 book](https://www.bain.com/contentassets/29f74ec417fa4e36a1d7d7e7479badc5/loyalty_rules_chapter_one.pdf)[Loyalty Rules!](https://www.bain.com/contentassets/29f74ec417fa4e36a1d7d7e7479badc5/loyalty_rules_chapter_one.pdf) states: "An increase in customer retention rates of 5 percent increases profits by 25 percent to 95 percent." He presents it as the bottom line of his earlier book, *The Loyalty Effect* .[Bain's own 2001 brief](https://media.bain.com/Images/BB_Prescription_cutting_costs.pdf) is more cautious, saying only that in financial services, "a 5% increase in customer retention produces more than a 25% increase in profit." A[2014](https://hbr.org/2014/10/the-value-of-keeping-the-right-customers)[Harvard Business Review](https://hbr.org/2014/10/the-value-of-keeping-the-right-customers)[article](https://hbr.org/2014/10/the-value-of-keeping-the-right-customers) later repeated the range as Bain research, with no industry attached. The range is real. What dropped off on the way is the scope behind it.


**"It costs five times more to acquire a customer than to retain one."** Keiningham, Vavra, Aksoy and Wallard traced this in[Loyalty Myths](https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/publication/2003-08/Ipsos_Loyalty_Myth_8_Excerpt.pdf) (Wiley). The earliest sources they found attribute it to the Technical Assistance Research Project (TARP) in the late 1980s. A 1990 *Harvard Business Review* article, "The Profitable Art of Service Recovery," then lent it credibility. Their verdict: "the reality is far more complex." The ratio shifts with a product's life-cycle stage. The most expensive customers to retain are often the most profitable. The 2014 *Harvard Business Review* summary widened it again, to "five to 25 times."


**"95% of AI pilots fail."** MIT's Project NANDA published "The GenAI Divide: State of AI in Business 2025" in July 2025. It reported that 95% of organizations were getting zero return from generative AI. The report drew on a review of more than 300 publicly disclosed AI initiatives, structured interviews with representatives of 52 organizations, and survey responses from 153 senior leaders at four industry conferences. Success meant a marked and sustained productivity or profit-and-loss impact. Wharton's Kevin Werbach,[quoted by Futuriom](https://www.futuriom.com/articles/news/why-we-dont-believe-mit-nandas-werid-ai-study/2025/08) , said: "I've read through the document multiple times, and I still can't understand where it comes from."


The "more than 80% of AI projects fail" figure has a stranger history. RAND's 2024 report on AI project failure opens with "[By some estimates, more than 80 percent of AI projects fail](https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RRA2680-1.html) ." The estimate it cites is a 2022 *Fortune* article. RAND's own research was 65 interviews with AI practitioners. RAND never measured the 80%.


## Why does an unsourced statistic hurt a CX business case?


**The unsourced number is usually the biggest term in the model.** A revenue-at-risk estimate built on a 26x silent-customer multiplier is mostly multiplier. If that term has no evidence, the model has none either.


**Finance teams check.** The people approving CX budgets trace inputs for a living. One bad citation gives them a reason to discount every other number on the slide, including the good ones.


**It moves the argument to the wrong place.** Once a stat is challenged, the meeting becomes a debate about the stat. The actual question, which customer problem to fix first, doesn't get discussed.


**Some of these numbers are directionally right.** Retention does matter more than most levers. Gupta, Lehmann and Stuart's 2004 study in the[Journal of Marketing Research](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1509/jmkr.41.1.7.25084) examined five firms. They found that a 1% improvement in retention, margin or acquisition cost improves firm value by 5%, 1% and 0.1%, respectively. That's a stronger, better-sourced argument for retention than the folklore it replaces.


## What should CX teams cite instead?


Treat third-party statistics as context and your own feedback as evidence. An industry number tells a CFO the problem is plausible. Your own data tells them it's happening here, and how big it is.


That's Thematic's position on measuring CX: a defensible number beats an impressive one. Thematic ranks feedback themes by their[measured impact](https://getthematic.com/insights/link-feedback-themes-nps-csat-drivers) on a score such as[net promoter score (NPS)](https://getthematic.com/insights/ultimate-guide-to-net-promoter-score) , not by how often they're mentioned. Every theme traces back to the[verbatim comments](https://getthematic.com/insights/customer-feedback-analysis) underneath it, so a challenged number can be checked in the room. Mitre 10, a New Zealand home improvement retail cooperative, found this way that[stock availability issues were taking half an NPS point](https://getthematic.com/insights/humanising-hardware-how-mitre10-made-voice-of-customer-actionable-with-thematic) off its overall scores. That figure came from its own feedback. Nobody had to take a listicle's word for it.


For the external context you still need, use sources that publish a method:


- **Complaint behavior:** the National Customer Rage Survey, which states its sample and has run since 2003.
- **Retention economics:** Gupta, Lehmann and Stuart (2004), or the original Reichheld and Sasser (1990) with its industries attached.
- **AI adoption risk:** Gartner's dated forecasts, labeled as forecasts. In July 2024[Gartner predicted](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2024-07-29-gartner-predicts-30-percent-of-generative-ai-projects-will-be-abandoned-after-proof-of-concept-by-end-of-2025) that at least 30% of generative AI projects would be abandoned after proof of concept by the end of 2025.
- **Survey limits:** Pew Research Center, which found that "[response rate is an unreliable indicator of bias](https://www.pewresearch.org/methods/2017/05/15/what-low-response-rates-mean-for-telephone-surveys/) ."


## How do you check a CX statistic before you use it?


Run every number through five questions before it goes on a slide:


1. **Can you open the original?** Not a blog quoting it. The report, paper or dataset itself.
2. **Does the original contain the exact number?** Bain's 2001 retention brief says "more than 25%" for financial services, not "25% to 95%."
3. **What was measured, and on whom?** Industry, country, year, sample size. A 1990 study of service businesses isn't your SaaS business.
4. **Is it a measurement or a forecast?** "Will be abandoned by 2025" is a prediction. Quote it as one.
5. **Does the number have one origin or several?** When the same figure is credited to three different firms, treat it as unsourced.


If a statistic fails two of these, drop it. If it fails one, cite it with the scope attached. If it passes, keep the link in your speaker notes, because someone will ask.


## The short answer


The most popular customer experience statistics with no real source are "96% of unhappy customers never complain" and "only 1 in 26 customers complain." The "5x more to acquire than retain" ratio is a late-1980s estimate repeated as fact. The "25% to 95%" retention-profit range is Reichheld's own, quoted without the scope behind it. The AI pilot failure rates are either weakly derived or second-hand. Each has a better alternative, and the best alternative is usually your own feedback, measured by impact and traceable to the comments behind it.


Before your next[CX business case](https://getthematic.com/insights/roi-of-cx) goes to finance, open every citation on the slide. Anything you can't open, replace.
